bio.en: Eric Ries is the author of The Lean Startup—the most influential startup book of the past 15 years—and now of Incorruptible: Why Good Companies Go Bad and How Great Companies Stay Great, on protecting what founders build.
bio.zh: Eric Ries 是《精益创业》（过去 15 年最具影响力的创业著作）的作者，如今又推出《Incorruptible: Why Good Companies Go Bad and How Great Companies Stay Great》，讲述如何守护创始人所建立的事业。

summary.en: Eric connects his new book Incorruptible to The Lean Startup by framing the first as about building a successful company and the second as about protecting it from the 'force that no one controls'—the drift toward mediocrity that corrupts even winning organizations. He shares how he advised Anthropic's founders to bake AI-safety accountability into their charter, and argues that principled, harder-than-easy decision-making yields unexpected rewards while ROI-only thinking leads astray. The episode is a practical guide for founders on keeping control of what they've built and avoiding the fate of companies destroyed by their own success.
summary.zh: Eric 将新书《Incorruptible》与《精益创业》联系起来：前者讲如何打造一家成功的公司，后者讲如何保护它免遭“无人掌控、人人服从”的力量——那种把即便成功的组织也拖向平庸的引力。他分享了如何建议 Anthropic 的创始人把 AI 安全问责写入公司章程，并主张坚持原则、选择“更难但更对”的决策会带来意外回报，而只算 ROI 的思维会把人带偏。这期节目是为创始人提供的实用指南：守住自己建立的事业，避免被自身成功反噬的命运。

（00:07:25）：不只是创始人被解雇，尽管我们显然会谈到这个话题。但前几天，我和一些朋友出去吃晚餐。我们不在家乡，也不在常去的地方。有人说：“哦，有家餐厅，我已经好几年没去了，但那儿真的很棒。我们去试试吧。” 我们坐下用餐，他们刚吃一口就开始玩手机，我们说：“老兄，你太没礼貌了。为什么玩手机？”  “就一会儿，就一会儿。嗯，我猜得没错。” 他转过身来，说：“我能感觉到这家餐厅被私募基金收购了。我能尝出来。”  我把这个故事讲了很多次，很多人听后都说：“哦，我知道你说的是哪家餐厅。” 然后他们能列举出12家类似的餐厅。

First of all, why has this been going on for hundreds of years when we all think that the market selects for value creation, so this shouldn't happen, yet it happens all the time. But secondly, if it's inevitable, if it's caused by greed or age or size, why are there exceptions?
turns.zh: 没有，我只是好奇问问。哦，好吧。这下成了我最喜欢的例子了。真是太有趣了。我之前根本不知道这事。不过这种情况太常见了。当时我在采访一位自然食品品牌的创始人，产品名称就用了她的名字。我现在都记不清她的名字了。产品名称就是她的名字。后来她被投资者赶下台了，对方正要给我讲整个故事。我说：“让我猜猜接下来发生了什么。董事会为了追求更高的增长和利润，把她赶下台了。结果产品质量下降，客户愤怒，员工不满，现在市场份额还在下滑。”他说：“你怎么知道的？我以为你说你不了解这家公司。”（00:09:36）：这种模式太普遍了。我们甚至没有专门的术语来描述它。我们每天都在经历，却不知道该怎么称呼它。不过我知道该怎么称呼。我知道我们的祖父母会怎么称呼它。他们会称之为腐败。不是合法贿赂或挪用公款。不不。这就像你建一座桥。如果桥塌了，然后莱尼，我说你是个工程师，我会说：“莱尼，为什么我的桥塌了？”如果你说：“嗯，因为重力啊。”我会说：“老兄，谢谢你这个天才见解。”我理解从某种角度来说这没错。我们会说：“这不可避免啊，都是贪婪导致的。”我称之为财务重力。“当公司规模变大时，总会出现人性弱点……” “是啊，但我想知道为什么这座桥塌了？更重要的是，其他桥为什么没塌？” （00:10:21）：然后他们会说：“哦，为此我们需要研究荷载、荷载系数、风荷载、剪切应力。”我们仔细检查后，说：“哦，看，所有的金属螺栓都被腐蚀了。生锈了。难怪会塌了。” 然后如果你说：“嗯，我想建座新桥，但不想让这座桥塌。该怎么做？”你不会说：“嗯，重力啊，能怎么办呢？” 不不。你会说：“那下次为什么不换不锈钢螺栓，这样就不会生锈了？”  “哦，对，真是个好主意。”所以这本书探讨的是组织层面的“不锈钢”对应物。书的结构不像传统商业书籍，你应该也注意到了。它更像是一部悬疑小说，一个双重悬疑。首先，当我们都认为市场会选择价值创造时，为什么这种情况几百年来一直存在？按理说不该发生啊，但它却屡见不鲜。其次，如果这是不可避免的，如果是贪婪、年龄或规模导致的，那为什么会有例外情况？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You're actually going to give us answers and solutions because it sounds like, okay, this is impossible. But you actually have-
turns.zh: 你实际上会给我们答案和解决方案，因为听起来，这简直不可能。但你确实有——

turns.speaker: Eric Ries
turns.en: I promise.
turns.zh: 我保证。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... you have some answers for what founders can do. Real quick, I'll just say on the viral X thing, I'm not exactly sure if the toxins are real. There's a whole viral thing on it. I haven't looked into it super deeply.
turns.zh: ……你有一些关于创始人可以采取的措施的建议。说个简短的，我对那个病毒X事件不太确定。网上有很多相关讨论。我还没深入研究过。

turns.speaker: Eric Ries
turns.en: Okay. All right. We both have homework to do now because it's what you feed your kids. You care. I'm definitely worried. Definitely worried to hear that.
turns.zh: 好的。好吧。我们现在都有功课要做了，因为这关乎你给孩子吃的东西。你很在意。我肯定很担心。听到这个消息真的很担心。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to talk about two things that are probably in people's minds as they listen to this conversation and even think about buying your book. One is, okay, I am not going to let this happen to my company. This is-
turns.zh: 接下来我想谈谈两件事，这两件事可能正萦绕在听众心头，甚至在考虑购买你的书时也会浮现在脑海中。第一件事是，嗯，我绝不能让这种情况发生在我的公司身上。这——

turns.speaker: Eric Ries
turns.en: Oh, sure. Sure.
turns.zh: 哦，当然。当然。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... oh, other people, they're weak, maybe they're of loose values. The other is just like, do I really need to do this? There's so many companies that are killing it. I don't think they've done any of this. Why do I even need to pay attention to this? So maybe let's start with that first one or this idea of, and this is a core thesis of your book. This is not like an ethical values thing. This is a structural element of building businesses in the US.
turns.zh: ……哦，其他人可能很软弱，或许他们的价值观不端正。第二件事是，我真的有必要这么做吗？毕竟有很多公司经营得风生水起，我觉得他们根本没做过这些事。我为什么还要关注这些呢？或许我们先从第一点入手，或者说这就是你书中一个核心论点。这不是道德伦理层面的问题，而是美国商业发展的结构性要素。

turns.speaker: Eric Ries
turns.en: I'm going to make a claim that's going to sound radical, but I'll back it up. If you don't get this right, no other decision you make about your company will matter for the long term because you're not going to be the one making it. According to Harvard Law School, among venture-backed companies that have the standard best practices set up that you got from your lawyer, only 20% of founders are still the CEO three years after going public. Just statistically speaking, everyone's being told by their lawyers, their bankers, their VCs, everybody that you're the exception. It's not going to happen to you, but statistically speaking, you're much more likely to be in the 80% than the 20%. (00:12:48): I'll tell you one story in particular. A very hot company came to see me a year or two before their IPO. They were planning IPO and I built the long-term stock exchange. I've done a bunch of stuff that people come to me for advice about these things. They wanted advice. How can we structure the IPO? We want to think long-term, we're really a mission-driven company, et cetera, et cetera. And I was going through their governance documents. I said, "Oh, good. You have all the best practices. So you're totally like..." I was like, "The good news is you're so screwed you're going to have to do something. This is your [inaudible 00:13:15] guarantee to get this mess." And I had all the data and just like I do in the book, like, here are the examples, here are the case studies, here's the data, you need to know about this. And the founder was really concerned. He's like, "Okay, we're going to definitely do something about this. We're going to fix it up." (00:13:28): But then he called me back a few months later. He's like... I said, "Well, what are you going to do?" He's like, "You know what? I talked to my bankers, talked to my lawyers, talked to my CFO, talked to my GC, talked to my VCs, talked my growth VCs. You know what they all said? They all said, 'Man, Eric is such a downer. If he really believed in your vision, if he really saw how special you were, he wouldn't talk like that. You're the exception.'" I said, "Okay, man, good luck." This company went public, had a very successful IPO. A lot of people made a lot of money. And then five months into their IPO, a competitor gets acquired and the whole category, everyone freaks out. Stock price collapses and the founder is ousted after five months as a public company. Now, if you read stories about the company, people were like, "Oh, he made all these mistakes. Their business model sucked. The company..." Blah, blah, blah. (00:14:19): Did he make mistakes? I'm sure he did. Were there problems? I'm sure. But had he really earned so little grace that he only got five months, the same people saying that the business model is horribly flawed, they invested in the company five months ago. Had it really changed so much in five months? This is what's going on. These collapses are all around us and we're being told it's normal. This is just the way it has to be, but it's not. These are choices about the specific structures, cultural practices, the management practices we do on the inside and the structural, the governance practices we do on the outside. On both of them, were being told to do things that are incredibly weak. And again, if you think you're going to be the exception, think again.
turns.zh:
我要说一个听起来很激进的观点，但我会用数据来佐证。如果你在这件事上没做对，那么你未来对公司的任何决策都将失去长期意义，因为你很可能不再是公司的掌舵人。据哈佛法学院研究，在那些遵循标准最佳实践（这些实践通常来自律师建议）的风投支持公司中，上市三年后仍担任CEO的创始人仅占20%。从统计数据来看，每个人都被律师、银行家、风投们告知"你会是那个例外"。但从概率上看，你更有可能成为那80%的失败者，而不是20%的成功者。

（00:12:48）我要讲一个具体案例。有一家备受瞩目的公司在IPO前一两年来找我咨询。他们计划上市，我曾为其设计长期的股票交易所上市方案。他们向我寻求建议："如何设计IPO架构？我们以使命为导向，注重长期发展"等等。而当我翻阅他们的治理文件时，我说"不错，所有最佳实践都到位了。但你们注定要出问题"。我拿出数据，书中列举的案例研究一一呈现，但创始人却很担忧："好吧，我们必须行动了。"

（00:13:28）但几个月后他又联系我，表示"我们和律师、银行家、CFO、法务总监、风投们沟通过，他们都说'埃里克太悲观了。如果他真心相信你们的愿景，就会用积极语气沟通。你们是例外'。"我只能说"祝你们好运"。这家公司上市后IPO大获成功，许多人赚得盆满钵满。但上市五个月后，竞争对手被收购，整个行业陷入恐慌，股价暴跌，创始人仅五个月后就被赶下台。如今读到相关报道时，人们总说"他们犯了所有错误，商业模式糟糕透顶"之类。但他真的犯了这么多错误吗？肯定有问题。但如果他真的只获得了五个月的宽容期，而那些批评商业模式有严重缺陷的人五个月前还投资了这家公司，那问题又出在哪里？五个月内情况真的变化如此之大吗？这才是关键所在。这些崩盘事件随处可见，而人们却被告知这是正常现象。这根本不是必须接受的现状。这些问题关乎公司内部的具体架构、文化实践和管理方式，以及外部治理结构。我们被要求采取极其薄弱的措施。再说一次，如果你认为自己会是例外，那请再想想吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm excited to talk about what to do, these governance elements, but let's talk about this other critique that I imagine people have in their head of just like, is this like... Okay, I need to figure out product market fit first.
turns.zh: 我很兴奋能聊聊该怎么做，这些治理要素，但先来说说我猜大家心里可能存在的另一个疑虑：这就像……好吧，我得先搞清楚产品与市场的适配性。

turns.speaker: Eric Ries
turns.en: Yeah, yeah. Worry about it later.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊。先别管这些了，以后再说。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Exactly. There's so much more I need to do. The chances of this working are so low. Why am ... I have no time for anything else.
turns.zh: 没错。我还有太多事要做。这项目成功的可能性太低了。为什么我……我根本没时间做其他事了。

turns.speaker: Eric Ries
turns.en: Oh, totally. You said something interesting in the lead in which you said like, "Well, a lot of other companies seem to be killing it and they don't have these protections, so they're fine." I would actually check your math. So many times when people give me this argument, they were like, "Well, such and such company..." Someone was like, "Cloudflare, they are just a normal company. They don't do this stuff." I'm like, "Check your math, buddy. Cloudflare does many of the things that we're talking about. They're one of the examples in the book, so I picked that on purpose." A lot of companies that you don't necessarily instantly think of as do-gooder, mission-driven companies are actually very mission-driven in terms of how they're structured, and they are almost always protected by at least one of the governance structures from this book. So check your math. People used to tell me Costco was an example that wasn't protected, so much so that I was surprised to learn that it was embodied in a governance fortress. You'll be surprised. If you do the math, if you look into it, you'll be surprised. (00:16:07): But let's talk about the product market fit thing because this one is really interesting to me. Generally speaking, this is one of the most important ideas in the whole book. The most important question about how to protect a product is not what protections it needs, but when those protections need to be enacted. And it's basically like that old proverb about the best time to plant a tree was 40 years ago, but the next best time is now. It is always too early until it's too late. And I'll give you the example. I've seen this hundreds of times myself personally. So I've literally been in the room where this kind of stuff gets discussed and it starts like this. You're incorporating your company, you talk to your lawyer, "Hey, I want to have..." These are called mission protective provisions in the law. "I heard this guy on Lenny's podcast," and your lawyer's like, "Oh, not again. Another guy, right? How many good ideas from Lenny's podcast are you going to tell me about? Okay, fine. What's this one?" (00:16:59): "He told me I need to have mission protective provisions." He'll pat you on the head and be like, "Oh, that's sweet, honey. That's great. Yeah, get product market fit, get some success. Success is ultimately your source of leverage. Success will protect you. Don't worry about it." You say, "Okay, great. But just thanks for letting me know." Now you raise some money. You got these VCs on your board, say the same thing. They're like, "Yeah, I totally am with you. We're on the same page. We want the same thing you want. We invested because we believe in you as the founder. There's no need to do this now. Let's just do it later. Do it when it's the more appropriate time." Okay. (00:17:27): You got a growth round. Now you got these bold contrarian growth VCs on your board. And they're like, "I don't know. You might not want to be too different from everybody else. Might make it hard to raise money." You're like, "I thought you were a bold contrarian. What?" "Okay, don't worry about it now. We can always do it later." Now you're doing IPO prep. Now you got bankers and lawyers and you've got a GC and you got... And they're all like, "Yep, yep. This is a great thing to bundle with the IPO itself. You don't need to worry about it now. First, we got to land the plane, let's get our house in order." Blah, blah, blah. Anyway, I've actually been in the room where the founder sits with the CFO and now it's like IPO planning, roadshow. Here we go. It's go time. We're about to file the papers. (00:18:05): And the founder's like, "Hey, whatever happened to those mission protective provisions?" You're like, "I wanted to really make sure we had our customers could participate in our IPO and I want a broadly shared prosperity and I want this thing for our employees. I have all this good stuff I want to do. Did we do any of that stuff? I don't see it in the S1." The CFO's like, "Oh, you were serious about that? Oh, sorry, man. You should have said something. Now it's too late." You're like, "Wait a minute, but when I talked to you about it last year, you said it was too early." "Yeah, it was. But now it's too late." (00:18:34): Was it ever the right time? No, it is never the right time to do this. If you put this off, you will eventually find yourself in a situation where you can no longer do it. You will have lost the leverage. Success will not protect you because success is what makes you a target. That story I told you about the five months CEO got fired. That company, everyone who worked on that IPO, every banker, every lawyer, the CFO, everybody, they profited from all the transaction volume that that company generated on the way up and on the way down. They're all fine. They're all onto the next IPO. They're like carnivores. They're onto the next thing to feed on. Meanwhile, the customers, the employees, the people that cared about their company were not so lucky.
turns.zh:
哦，完全正确。你在开场时提到了一些有趣的观点，你说"嗯，很多其他公司似乎做得很好，他们没有这些保护措施，所以他们没事"。我其实想让你再检查一下你的逻辑。很多时候，当人们给我这种论点时，他们会说"嗯，比如某某公司……"有人说"Cloudflare只是个普通公司。他们不做这些事情。"我会说"检查一下你的逻辑吧，朋友。Cloudflare确实在做我们讨论的很多事情。他们是书中的例子之一，所以我特意选了他们。" 很多你不一定立即认为是善意、使命驱动型公司的公司，在其架构上实际上非常有使命感，而且他们几乎总是受到本书中至少一种治理结构的保护。所以检查一下你的逻辑吧。人们过去常告诉我Costco就是一个没有保护的例子，结果我惊讶地发现它实际上被包裹在一个治理堡垒中了。你会感到惊讶的。如果你仔细研究，你会很惊讶的。  

（00:16:07）：但让我们谈谈产品市场适配性这个问题，因为这对我来说真的很感兴趣。总的来说，这是整本书中最重要的概念之一。如何保护一个产品的最重要问题不是它需要什么保护措施，而是何时需要实施这些保护措施。这就像那句古老的谚语：种树的最佳时机是40年前，其次是现在。总是为时已晚，但未雨绸缪。让我举个例子。我自己就亲眼见过这种情况数百次了。所以我曾亲身参与过这种讨论的会议，通常是这样的过程。你正在注册公司，和你的律师谈话："嘿，我想在公司章程中加入……"这些在法律上被称为"使命保护条款"。"我在Lenny的播客上听说这个人提到过。" 你的律师会说："哦，又来了。又一个？你要告诉我多少个Lenny播客的好点子？好吧，那这又是什么鬼主意？" 你说："好吧，很好。但还是谢谢你告诉我。" 现在你筹集了资金。董事会里有风险投资人，他们也这么说："是的，我完全赞同你的观点。我们想法一致。我们和你一样。我们投资是因为相信你这个创始人。现在没必要做这些。以后再说吧。" 好吧。  (00:17:27)：你完成了增长轮融资。现在董事会里有那些大胆的反叛者型风险投资人。他们会说："我不知道。你可能不想和其他人太不一样。这可能会让你很难筹集资金。" 你会说："我以为你们是大胆的反叛者呢。什么？"  "好吧，现在先别管这个。以后再说吧。" 现在你在做IPO准备工作。有银行家、律师、总法律顾问……他们都会说："是的，是的。这和IPO本身捆绑在一起很棒。你现在不需要管这个。首先，我们得把事情搞定，理顺内部流程。" 等等等等。总之，我确实参加过创始人与CFO坐在一起的会议，现在已经进入IPO规划、路演阶段了。这里
开始行动了。是时候提交文件了。（00:18:05）创始人问：“嘿，那些使命保护条款怎么回事？”你回答：“我本想确保客户能参与我们的IPO，追求广泛的共同繁荣，造福员工。我还有好多好想法，但这些内容在S1文件里找不到啊。”首席财务官说：“哦，你是认真的啊？抱歉啊，你当时应该提出来的。现在太晚了。” 你反问：“等等，去年我跟你谈的时候，你说还太早。”“是啊，但现在确实太晚了。” （00:18:34）这事儿有合适的时机吗？根本没有！拖延只会让局面恶化，最终失去主动权。成功不会保护你，因为成功本身就是目标。去年那个被解雇的CEO，公司里的每个参与IPO的人，银行家、律师、CFO，全都从公司股价上涨和下跌期间产生的交易量中获利。他们安然无恙，继续追逐下一笔IPO。这些投机者就像食肉动物，寻找下一个猎物。而那些关心公司的客户、员工，却未能幸免于难。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Damn. That hit me. That hit me right in the heart. And it's so obvious just how personal and important this is to you. It's clear you've just seen this happen again and again and you're just like-
turns.zh: 天哪。这句话太戳心了。这句话直击我的心坎。显然，这件事对你来说意义非凡，私人性极强。很明显，你目睹过这种情况一次又一次发生，而你现在——

turns.speaker: Eric Ries
turns.en: Oh yeah. I've been in the room where it happens. Yeah. The proverbial room.
turns.zh: 哦，对啊。我也曾身处那种事态发生的房间。没错，就是那个众所周知的房间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So let's talk about what people should do and we'll poke around in different directions. What's the broad stroke solution to this? And then what are some, say, three things, say an early stage founder should do this week, next week?
turns.zh: 好吧。那我们来聊聊人们该怎么做，再从不同角度探讨一下。针对这个问题，整体性的解决方案是什么？然后再说说，比如说，初期创业者这周、下周应该做哪三件事？

turns.speaker: Eric Ries
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Okay. So broadly speaking, there is a blueprint. I promise when we talk about the horrors of living in late stage capitalism, it's easy to get depressed and just be like... I mean, literally part one of this book is called The Shape of the Abyss. So I'm not trying to sugarcoat it. This is quite grim. And if you haven't studied these case studies, if you don't know the story of Whole Foods and what happened to it, if you don't know the story of Vectura, you don't know these stories, they're really grim and it's important to grapple with what happened so that it doesn't happen to you, so that you're prepared. But it can feel like we're so helpless. But as I said, this is a double mystery, not just why does this happen, but how can there be exceptions to a rule that's inevitable? (00:20:25): So let me just tell one more story and then we'll get really into the tactical details because I want some stories that we can use. It's our fact set, our database to draw these principles out. And so the blueprint, I'll give you the spoiler alert. I just mentioned before, ethos plus integrity, that's our formula. Ethos meaning internal alignment, character, choices, integrity, meaning the structure to resist to keep ourselves aligned with human flourishing. Let's go back in time a little further this time. We're going to go to 1920 Denmark. I want to tell you about a woman named Marie Krogh. She was one of the first doctors to practice in Denmark, like a credentialed doctor. She was a big advocate for women's medical education and she lived a very cool life in her own right. But she's famous today mostly because of her husband, August, who had just won the Nobel Prize, who was a very famous scientist. (00:21:14): And she, unfortunately, right around the same time, got diagnosed with a fatal illness, an illness for which there was no known cure at that time. It was called diabetes. So she gets this death sentence right as he's winning the Nobel Prize and he asks her, would she come with him to North America for his lecture tour anyway? And she says yes. So the two of them travel to North America. He's going around talking to scientists about his Nobel Prize. And one night at dinner, Marie is sitting next to a scientist who tells her, "Hey, actually in Canada, there are these researchers who have figured out a new technology to isolate a substance called insulin, a potential cure for diabetes." So Marie convinces her husband we should extend our trip, go to Canada, see this thing for themselves. They do. They are both scientists, so they instantly understand the implications. (00:22:03): This could not only save Marie's life, but millions more. So they talked to the Canadians, "Could we commercialize this technology?" And the Canadians said they're open to it, but everyone involved has a concern. We've been talking so far about the concern of being forced out of your company or having it taken away from you. That is one danger, but there's also the temptation to harvest what others plant, the temptation to exploit, to extract instead of creating new value. They were worried about that. Now Lenny, I want you to imagine this scenario with me, okay? Imagine that I depend on you for a lifesaving cure. I have diabetes, you're the only maker of insulin in the world. In that case, I would want you to charge me a fair price. Very much so. It's both morally right, fair, but also I want you to have every incentive possible to keep making the drug, otherwise I might die. (00:22:52): Okay. But what if one day you wake up and you're like, "Wait a second, I don't have to charge Eric a fair price." Or you have investors whispering in your ear, "Lenny, you don't have to charge him a fair price. You can charge him anything you want." That's what I would live in fear of. So decades before Martin Shkreli actually did this as a business strategy, the Kroghs and the Canadian scientists, they were worried that this might happen to their new company. So when they went back to Denmark to create this company, which they called the Nordisk Insulinlaboratorium, they incorporated it using this very particular structure. It is a for-profit company. It does have outside investors, but it is owned, governed by a nonprofit foundation, a two-tiered structure that's called an industrial foundation in the literature. And if Nordisk Insulinlaboratorium sounds familiar, it should. This is the predecessor company to what we today call Novo Nordisk, one of the largest companies in the world. (00:23:47): And what's so interesting to me about this story is this structure has endured and protected the ethos of scientific integrity of Novo Nordisk for more than a hundred years. Meanwhile, so many of the best practices that your lawyers, your bankers, whoever advisors you have, they're going to be pushing best practices on you that are younger than the trees in your local park. And so what I want for everyone who's listening to this, founders, product managers, leaders, board members, I don't care. The next time someone comes to you pushing a best practice and you're like, "Oh, I guess I have to do it this way because we live in an ROI dominated culture. We have to stack rank by ROI," or whatever the practice is, I want you to be like, well, that person sounds very smart. They're very well credentialed. They went to business school or whatever. (00:24:31): But ask yourself, are you sure they're smarter than a Nobel laureate? Because August and Marie worked this out a hundred years ago and it has held so many attacks. In fact, I tell a story in the book and Lenny, I know you're going to think I'm exaggerating or at least some of your listeners are going to think, oh, Eric is an exaggerator. I promise you this is a 100% true story. The trustees of the nonprofit foundation once had to intervene to protect the for profit from this exact temptation to want to sell it out. And I won't get into the whole story. They did the right thing in this case-

是啊，是啊，是啊。好的。总的来说，有个蓝图。我保证，当我们谈论晚期资本主义的恐怖时，人们很容易陷入沮丧，觉得……我的意思是，书的第一部分就叫《深渊的形状》。所以我不想粉饰太平。这情况确实很严峻。如果你没研究过这些案例研究，如果你不知道全食超市的遭遇，如果你不了解Vectura公司的故事，这些案例都相当令人沮丧。重要的是，要深刻理解这些教训，避免重蹈覆辙，未雨绸缪。但有时我们会感到无能为力。正如我所说，这是一个双重谜团——不仅要解释为何会出现这种情况，更要探究在不可避免的规则中为何会有例外。（00:20:25）：所以让我再讲一个故事，然后我们就深入探讨战术细节了。因为我需要一些案例作为支撑我们的论点。这是我们的事实基础、数据库，用来提炼这些原则。那么蓝图是什么呢？我提前透露一下，我之前提到的伦理+诚信，就是我们的公式。伦理意味着内在的统一、品格、选择，诚信则意味着抵抗外界干扰，坚守人类繁荣的准则。这一次让我们回溯更久的历史。让我们回到1920年的丹麦。我要讲一个叫玛丽·克罗格的女性。她是丹麦首批获得行医资格的医生之一，也是女性医学教育的积极倡导者，她本人的生活也相当精彩。但如今她最出名的原因是她的丈夫奥古斯特——这位刚刚获得诺贝尔奖的著名科学家。（00:21:14）：不幸的是，差不多在他获奖的同时，玛丽被诊断出了一种当时无药可治的致命疾病——糖尿病。当他得知获奖消息时，玛丽正面临绝症诊断，但他仍邀请她随自己前往北美进行巡讲。玛丽答应了。于是两人启程前往北美。奥古斯特在各地向科学家们讲述诺贝尔奖相关事宜。某晚晚餐时，玛丽坐在一位加拿大科学家旁边，得知加拿大研究者已研发出分离胰岛素的技术，或许能治愈糖尿病。玛丽说服丈夫延长行程前往加拿大亲自验证。作为科学家，他们立刻意识到技术的潜在价值。（00:22:03）：这项技术不仅能救玛丽一命，还可能拯救数百万人。他们与加拿大科学家商讨商业化事宜。加拿大人表示愿意合作，但各方都担忧潜在风险。我们此前讨论了被迫退出公司或失去控制权的风险，这只是其中一种危险。另一种诱惑是掠夺他人成果、剥削而非创造新价值。他们深知其中的利害关系。现在，莱尼，我想请你和我一起设想这个场景：假设我依赖你生产救命药物。我患糖尿病，而你是我全球唯一的胰岛素制造商。在这种情况下，我肯定希望你能收取合理价格。这既是道德正确，也是公平交易，但更重要的是，我需要你有足够动机持续生产药物，否则我可能会死去。（00:22:52）：好的。但如果某天你醒来后突然想：“等等，
其次，我没必要给埃里克一个公平的价格。” 或者有投资者在你耳边低语：“莱尼，你不必给他一个公平的价格。你想收多少就收多少。” 这正是我所担心的风险。因此，早在马丁·什克雷利将此作为商业策略之前，克罗格斯家族和加拿大科学家们就担心这种情况可能会发生在他们的新公司身上。于是，当他们回到丹麦创立这家名为北欧胰岛素实验室的公司时，他们采用了一种特殊的公司结构。这是一家营利性公司，确实有外部投资者，但它由非营利基金会所有和管理——这种双层结构在文献中被称为工业基金会。如果北欧胰岛素实验室听起来耳熟，那应该不奇怪。它正是我们今天所熟知的全球大型企业之一——诺和诺德的前身公司。（00:23:47） 这个故事最让我感兴趣的是，这种结构在过去一个多世纪里一直延续并保护着诺和诺德的科学诚信精神。与此同时，许多你身边的律师、银行家或顾问推行的所谓最佳实践，其历史可能比你当地公园里的树木还要短暂。对我来说，希望听众中的每一位——无论是创始人、产品经理、领导者还是董事会成员——都能明白：下次有人向你推荐某种最佳实践时，你若认为“因为我们生活在一个以投资回报率为导向的文化中，必须以ROI为标准进行排名”之类的，我想你应该反问：这个人听起来很聪明，资质深厚，上过商学院之类的。但请问自己，你确定他们比诺贝尔奖得主更聪明吗？因为奥古斯特和玛丽早在一百年前就想出了这个方案，并成功抵御了无数次攻击。事实上，我在书中讲述了一个故事，莱尼，我知道你会觉得我在夸大其词，或者至少你的一些听众会认为“埃里克是个夸大其词的人”。但我向你保证，这完全是真实的故事。非营利基金会的受托人曾不得不介入，保护这家营利性公司免受出售股权的诱惑。我就不详细讲述整个故事了。在这种情况下，他们做出了正确的选择——

(00:27:43): But I'll just, for the sake of us having a hypothetical that we can do, I would always tell ... We go around the room, Some of them are on Zoom, everyone puts in the chat and someone will be like, Halliburton. And someone else will be like ... Increasingly, tech companies are showing up on these lists now, which when I was younger, that would never have been the case. But now you somehow see tech companies there. Some will see Monsanto or you see ... Or some private equity fund. People are mad about something, they can name a company usually. So it's not hard to find examples. (00:28:09): Now, my father was a pulmonologist growing up. So I was raised that Philip Morris is the most evil company in the world. So we'll just use that as our hypothetical just for the sake of argument today. If you think Philip Morris is great and you have different values, whoever's listening, fine. You pick the company you really would never, ever, ever want to have to work for no matter what. (00:28:29): Now, I ask people to imagine the company they currently work at. Philip Morris shows up one day and says, "I'd like to buy this company from you for $1 more per share than it's currently worth." You selling? Most people are like, "Hell no. Hell no, I'm not selling." (00:28:51): One person once asked me, "Well, what are they going to use it for?" Oh, sorry, to be clear, they're going to use it to sell cigarettes to children. Now you selling? Yeah. No. No deal. Obviously, F no, but I can't actually say on your podcast the kind of things people say when they were presented with this because there might be children listening. Okay? People get real upset at this idea. (00:29:10): And when we talk about ... I'm like, "Okay, well, did you know that according to the legal documents you, yourself, signed, your company's literal charter that you have right now, and this is not some hypothetical future thing. You've already put in motion a rule that says you have a fiduciary duty to say yes in this situation." People are so outraged. They're like, "That cannot be right. My lawyer, my guy, he would never have done that to me." I'm like, "Call him up, ask him if what I say is true and call me back." (00:29:51): So occasionally though, people will say, Eric, you are exaggerating. Yes, that can happen, but come on, does that really happen in real life? Is that something I really need? I'm Johnny at product marketplace, do I have to worry about it? (00:30:03): So before you tell me I'm exaggerating, I want you to consider this from the perspective of the founder scientists of the Vectura Corporation. (00:30:49): There's this company. This is what happened. Philip Morris said they wanted to diversify beyond nicotine. And they were like, "Oh, we know a lot about inhaling things. (00:31:06): So here were the three choices that were facing the Vectura board. They had this bid from Philip Morris for 165 pence per share. But the only people that mattered were the people on the board of directors of the Vectura Corporation. They had, I think, two meetings about it and they just said, "Our hands are tied. We have a fiduciary duty to accept the highest bid." Which they did. (00:31:51): So yes, if you think I was exaggerating, I was. I said it was a dollar per share. In real life, it was more like 15 cents a share. So let's find out what happened next, shall we? Can you guess?
turns.zh:
太痛苦了。我再讲个故事吧。我们一直讲些开心的故事。让我讲个不怎么开心的故事吧。（00:27:13）：多年来我一直在做这样一个练习，我会问创始人或各级领导者：“听着，在我们深入细节之前，先告诉我，你认为世界上最邪恶的公司是哪家？”有时他们能立刻想到答案。他们会说：“哦，我知道。”但有些人会问：“你说‘邪恶’是什么意思？”我说：“就是那种无论出多少钱你都绝不会去为之工作的公司。你能感觉到他们在搞鬼。”每个人脑海里都有这样一家公司。我知道你们可能不愿说出心目中的‘邪恶’公司，理解的，没关系。（00:27:43）：但为了举个假设的例子，我通常会让大家……我们围成一圈，有些人用Zoom参加，大家在聊天区输入答案，有人会说‘哈里伯顿’。还有人会说……如今科技公司越来越多地出现在这类名单上。我年轻时绝不会想到会这样，但现在你确实能看到科技公司上榜。有人会提到孟山都，或是某家私募基金。人们对某些事物不满时，通常能说出几家公司。所以找例子并不难。（00:28:09）：我父亲曾是一名肺科医生，所以我从小就认为菲利普·莫里斯是最邪恶的公司。今天我们就以菲利普·莫里斯为例进行假设讨论。如果你认为菲利普·莫里斯很棒，价值观不同，听众随意。但现在你必须说出心目中无论如何都绝不会为之工作的公司。（00:28:29）：现在让我大家想象自己目前工作的公司。如果你是创始人，你就是公司；如果你是员工，你也是公司。但你珍视的公司，想象一下，菲利普·莫里斯某天出现，说：“我愿意以每股比当前价值高1美元的价格从你手中收购这家公司。”你会卖吗？大多数人会说：“绝对不卖。绝不卖。”（00:28:51）：有人曾问我：“他们要用这笔钱做什么？” 哦，对不起，明确一点，他们会用这笔钱向儿童销售香烟。现在你还卖吗？是的，不卖。没门儿。显然，绝对不行，但我不能在你的播客上透露人们在面对这种假设时会说什么，因为可能有孩子在听。好吗？人们对这个想法非常愤怒。他们会说：“这太不公平了。我的律师，我的顾问绝不会这么对我。” 我说：“打电话问问他我说的是否属实，然后回电告诉我。” 他们会说：“他说他是在帮我忙，给我提供最佳实践文件，让我更容易融资。” 是啊。

（00:29:10）不过偶尔会有人说，我埃里克，你太夸张了。是的，这种情况可能存在，但说真的，现实中真有这种事吗？我真的需要担心吗？我是Product Marketplace的约翰尼，我需要为此担忧吗？（00:30:03）：所以在你们说我夸张之前，我希望你们从以下角度考虑这个问题：
以下是Vectura公司创始科学家们的视角。Vectura是一家英国公司，由巴斯大学衍生而来。他们开发用于治疗哮喘和慢性阻塞性肺病（COPD）的吸入疗法产品——大家都见过吸入器，对吧？这是一家医药公司。他们非常成功，成功融资并在伦敦证券交易所上市。然而有一天，菲利普·莫里斯公司试图收购他们。我之所以知道这个故事，是因为多年来我一直用菲利普·莫里斯作为例子。研究这本书时，我好奇地问克劳德：“有没有公司真的被菲利普·莫里斯收购过？”我随口一问，却没想到他反问：“你是在问Vectura吗？”我连忙追问：“快给我讲讲！”  
（00:30:49）：事情是这样的。菲利普·莫里斯称想在尼古丁领域之外实现多元化。他们表示：“我们对吸入疗法很在行，所以收购一家吸入器公司……”听闻此消息的普通人都会疑惑：“这根本说不通！大型烟草公司收购健康公司？这太离谱了吧！”  
（00:31:06）：Vectura董事会面临三个选择：菲利普·莫里斯出价每股165便士；一家美国私募基金出价每股155便士；第三个选项是保持独立，因为公司运营良好。英国公众对此强烈抗议，英国胸科协会恳求拒绝收购。任何稍作思考的人都能看出这将是一个极具毁灭性的决策。但关键决策者是Vectura的董事会。他们召开了两次会议，最终宣称：“我们受托责任必须接受最高报价。” 结果他们选择了菲利普·莫里斯。  
（00:31:51）：没错，如果你觉得我夸大其词，那确实如此。我之前说的是每股一美元，现实中价格更接近每股15便士。接下来会发生什么呢？大家猜猜看？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Not great.
turns.zh: 情况不容乐观。

turns.speaker: Eric Ries
turns.en: Philip Morris spent £1.1 billion to buy Vectura. Within three years, they had taken a $900 million write down and disposed of the company for peace parts, it doesn't exist anymore. These are the stakes, this is what happens. And I can't tell you, I feel like Perry Mason sometimes when people are like, "I would never do that." I'm like, "Okay, I hear you have good intentions, but can I please see your signature on the document?" Oh, look, Delaware charters are public record, by the way. If you ever want to know, if a friend is a lawyer, just you want to know if a company has a mission or if this is going to happen to them, just pull the charter. You can just read it. Read it for yourself. I'm like, "Is this your signature right here? You, yourself, sign this document and you don't even understand how your company works." (00:32:46): The stakes I think are significantly existential, especially now that we're entering an age, the age of wonders. The age of technologies that are incredibly powerful, that have planet scale consequences to them. I think a lot of founders, a lot of product people, they want to build a product that they can be proud of. That their grandkids will be happy to hear that that's how the family fortune was made. And I know a lot of people that are incredibly rich and so miserable. Because the thing, their baby, it got ruined, it got destroyed. Why are we doing this?
turns.zh:
菲利普·莫里斯花了11亿英镑收购Vectura。三年内，他们就计提了9亿美元的减值准备，并将该公司出售用于零部件生产，如今它已不复存在。这就是现实局面，这就是现实世界的规则。我无法详述此事，有时听人说"我绝不会那么做"，我会回应："好吧，我知道你本意是好的，但能否请你把签名放在文件上？"哦，顺便说一句，特拉华州的公司章程是公开记录的。如果你想了解某家公司的使命，或是想预知自己会不会遭遇类似命运，只要调出章程看看就行了。自己读一读吧。我会问："这签名是你的吗？你自己签的文件，却连公司的运作机制都不清楚。"
（00:32:46）：我认为当下我们正步入一个充满奇迹的时代，科技的力量无比强大，甚至能影响整个星球的命运。许多创业者、产品开发者都想打造令自己引以为傲的产品，让子孙后代能因家族财富的来源而倍感自豪。但我认识许多极其富有却备受折磨的人，因为他们的"心血结晶"被毁掉了。我们为何要如此执着？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Let's talk about what to actually do. And this is going to be a kind of a high level overview. Obviously by the book, if you really want to get serious about this stuff coming out May 26th that all [inaudible 00:33:29] -
turns.zh: 好的，接下来聊聊实际行动吧。这将是一次高层次的概述。当然，如果你想深入研究5月26日发布的相关内容，[00:33:29未听清]——

turns.speaker: Eric Ries
turns.en: May 26. Yes, thank you.
turns.zh: 5月26日。是的，谢谢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Anywhere you buy books. Talk about what we should do. And I just want to plant the seed of OpenAI is probably on people's minds as they hear this idea of building a nonprofit.
turns.zh: 任何购书平台。探讨我们该如何行动。我只想抛出一个想法：当人们听到建立非营利组织的概念时，OpenAI很可能浮现在他们的脑海中。

turns.speaker: Eric Ries
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. We'll get there. And obviously in the book, I tell the Anthropic story where I played a bit part. So we'll get to all that. We'll get to all that. (00:33:43): But let's start with the easy stuff first because AI is kind of like the humanities final exam. You've heard that joke. These issues are so amplified in AI, of course we have to get it right. I think it's incredibly important and I've done what I can to set us on that proper path. But it's easier to see it, I think, in simpler businesses. OpenAI's business is insanely complicated. So let's look at it in some simpler examples first. (00:34:10): Let's start with the principle I call harder is easier. This is the leadership principle that anybody can adopt. There's nobody who's not ... You tell me you have no power whatsoever. Everyone's got some influence. And if you have any influence at all, you can adopt this principle. (00:34:28): When I talk to people about business, I don't care if I'm talking to two guys in a garage, founders, or I'm talking to super boards or CEO, C-suite, whatever. Everyone always says to me, just what you were saying a minute ago, it's like, "Man, Eric, business is already so hard. Now you want me to do extra? Now I got to worry about the Vectura thing and this other stuff. Man, I'm already just trying to get through the day. It's so hard." (00:34:53): But I think this is a basically backwards way of looking at it. Because I ask people, could it be, just consider the possibility that one of the reasons you're finding business so hard is that nobody trusts you. If they trusted you, maybe it would be a little bit easier. Now, actually, this is not a supposition, we have really good evidence. Companies where their employees trust them, spend way less time on employee communications. They have much better alignment. Everyone's kind of rowing in the same directions. When customers trust you, of course, you have way higher loyalty, your cost of customer acquisition is lower. But also customers more likely to stick with you after you make a mistake. They're more likely to try your new product. So many people are like, "God, customers are so fickle. They have no loyalty. They only care about the slick marketing from our competitors." But maybe because you view these things as extra is part of the problem. (00:35:46): So harder is easier is a principle that says, if you're willing to do the work upfront to commit to quality, to design, to ethics, to integrity, to safety, whatever the thing, I don't want to tell you what your values are, you tell me what they are. If you're willing to be principled in your decision making, you will get these unexpected rewards. Now, you can't do it for the reward or it doesn't work. You have to do it for the thing itself. Trustworthiness is the most underrated asset in all of business. And the things that create trustworthiness, by definition, stack rank to the bottom if we do it by ROI. Because doing the right thing has intangible rewards, but tangible costs. (00:36:28): So let me give you another story. Because now we've been talking about lofty stuff, and I want to talk about something super practical. And I mentioned Cloudflare before. So let me actually tell the Cloudflare story. I like Cloudflare because Matthew Prince and his co-founders, they were really anti-consulting BS talk. In the early days, they came out of Harvard Business School and so they were traumatized. They were just like, "No, I don't want to hear about mission statement. I don't want to hear about values. We are making a firewall and putting it in the cloud. It's not that complicated. We don't want to hear it." So for years, they had no mission statement. (00:37:03): And this is a critical point. As leaders, we get so focused on value statement, mission statements. We forget the mission statement is not the mission. The map is not the territory. Mission is an emergent property of the living superorganism of the thing we're birthing. Okay? It's not something you can slap on with a label. You have to build it in. You want to have a company that stands for quality, you got to build quality in from the inside. Deming taught this in the 40s. This is not some new idea. This is a critical idea. This is what craftsmanship really means. Okay. (00:37:32): So we know that Cloudflare had a mission because quite often they would do this harder is easier stuff. And without even really knowing why. There's a very famous example in their history where pro-democracy protesters, I want to say ... I forget what nation state they were pissing off. I better not say, in case I get it wrong. Pissing off some nation state, were having state-sponsored hackers trying to take their websites down so they couldn't coordinate their pro-democracy protests. (00:37:59): They were going around Silicon Valley begging big tech companies to help them defend their websites. No one would do it. All these big mega companies, even Google were just like, "I'm too scared." And so Cloudflare, the tiny startup is like, "We'll do it." These were free tier customers. They weren't even paying any money. And they're like, "Yes, we will incur the wrath of nation state level hackers to protect you because it's the right thing to do for no reward whatsoever." That was just the kind of company they were. (00:38:26): So anyway, a couple years in, they're having lunch and one of the engineers says, "You know why I like working at this company? I just feel like it's the first place I've worked where we're trying to make a better internet." And everyone on the table's like, "Yeah, make a better internet." Someone asked Matthew, "Oh, is that our mission statement?" Smack. "No, we don't have a mission statement. I know what you're talking about? No." (00:38:46): But it actually was. Over time, the engineers, people who worked there kept saying, "Make a better internet." That was how we talk about it. And eventually the founders had to be convinced, "Okay, let's adopt this as our mission statement," which they did. That's their mission statement to this day. They had to eventually adopt formal values. As you get bigger, these things really matter. It matters that you document those emergent properties, otherwise how are people supposed to know what they are? Their number one value, by the way, is be principled, which is the ultimate harder is easier move. (00:39:14): So this all sounds great. It's fun to have values. It's fun to have a mission statement when it doesn't cost you anything. But sometimes it can be very expensive. It can make your life a lot harder. That's why we call the principle harder is easier. One day, a junior engineer, not like some senior executive or anything, walks into Matthew Prince's office and he says, "Boss, isn't our mission statement to make a better internet?" When you're a CEO, any conversation that starts this way is definitely going to be extra work for you. So you're like, "What is it now?" It's like, "Well, you were saying at the board meeting that our number one driver of revenue, the thing that causes people to upgrade from our free to premium plans," this is a few years ago now, "Is web encryption, SSL encryption. You said that makes sense because SSL encryption is expensive to offer, we can't offer it for free. We have to get the certificates and pay for them. We have to do all this extra cryptographic stuff as compute ... We have scarce compute, da-da-da-da-da." "Sure." (00:40:08): "But boss, wouldn't a better internet be an encrypted internet?" And he's like, "Yes. So what's your point?" So if it would be better, why are we giving it away for free? And so many people have heard this story. If you've ever been a middle manager in a company, okay, you know this, you're just like, "Oh my God. Every day someone walks into your office that's like, here you boss, let's give our product away for free for no reason." Your job as a middle manager is to be like, "No, we have a strategy. Get back on the strategy. Redirect. Thank you for your buy-in and your input, but we have a job to do." (00:40:44): So everyone's expecting Matthew to react that way and would be the most normal thing in the world. This is our most profitable product and you're saying we should give it away for free, get lost. No. Matthew told me once I saw it, I couldn't unsee it. And he uttered the three keywords, he said, "Let's figure it out." Figure it out. This is the leadership principle I think is so powerful, the figure it out principle. (00:41:08): If you're committed to something, you stand for quality or whatever, it's going to make life harder. The best leaders, the ones I really admire, they revel in it. They love the difficulty. Because every time you have one of these impossible dilemmas, it's a chance to teach what you really stand for. So Matthew insisted the whole team rally to figure out how to give encryption away for free. Now they couldn't just give it away for free. He's like, "Bankrupting the company won't achieve the mission." We had to find a way to make it sustainable. And I won't go through all the technical details of how they managed to get the cost. They had to hand roll their own software and assembly language. They had to do these complicated biz dev deals with certificate authorities. They figured out how to do it and they drove their own cost down. (00:41:48): Now, keep in mind that at any time ... First of all, I could have used the difficulty as an excuse, "Oh, it's too hard. We can't do it." Give up. Once they did it, they could have said, "Wait a minute, this is just free margin. We can make our costs lower and then we just get free money." When they shipped it, they had to report to their board on what happened. The conversion rates for premium product went down. So they could easily have bailed out at that point, but they didn't. They stuck with it because this is what we stand for. (00:42:15): Now, of course, it's a happy ending story. The top of funnel increased by an order of magnitude. In fact, to this day, people still talk about how Cloudflare is like the reason you take for granted we have an encrypted internet. The trust that they gained is the reason why they're a $70 billion company today. But most leaders, when asked to defend their principles, can't do it. Because they've been taught ROI-based thinking, they've been taught shareholder primacy, they've been taught that that's the path of maximum profitability. (00:42:43): To give you an easy contrast, Andrew Mason, the founder of Groupon once told me this story. Everyone remember Groupon? Maybe not now. It's kind of fallen out of public consciousness, but there was this time where Groupon was one of the fastest growing private companies in America. It was powered by a daily email with a cool deal. And the whole thing was you got one email a day from Groupon. They went public on the one email a day, that's how successful it was. (00:43:06): And I remember he told me this story one day, his executives and employees started coming into his office and they'd be like, "You know, boss, we need to make the quarter. We need to make more money. We're a public company now. We don't want to be better than one email. Have you considered two emails?" And he was like, "No. One email a day," he's like, "That's our whole thing." But he said, over time, they ground him down and they kept saying, they were using language that sounds kind of lean start-upy. Shouldn't we do an experiment? Shouldn't we look at the data? What about the IR ... it's just like, what about the ROI? And so he's like, "All right, fine. We'll run the experiment." (00:43:38): He ran the experiment. Two emails a day makes more money. So he couldn't say no. And everything was fine for several months until someone came to his office and said, "You know, boss, you know what'd be better than two email? We should send three emails." And next thing you know, they're sending eight emails. And this is not just Groupon. I have had so many CEOs tell me this exact story about email frequency. Email frequency is like, for some reason, the tip of the spear where it's like, we don't really have any way to defend doing the right thing here. So we did the wrong thing. That destroyed the whole company. But in the short term, we made a bunch of money. (00:44:13): So if you can stick to the harder is easier principle, that is the first line of defense against losing whatever it is that makes a company special.
turns.zh:
是啊，是啊。我们会解决这些问题的。当然，在书中我讲述了自己参与的"人类中心主义"故事。所以这些内容我们都会讲到。（00:33:43）但我们先从简单点儿的开始吧，因为人工智能就好比期末考试。你们都听过那个笑话——在人工智能领域，这些问题被放大得尤其严重，所以我们必须把它做好。我认为这非常重要，我也尽力让大家走上正确的道路。但我觉得在更简单的业务中，这点更容易看清。OpenAI的业务极其复杂。所以我们先看看更简单的例子。

（00:34:10）首先，我要讲一个我称之为"越难越容易"的原则。这是一个任何人都能采用的领导原则。没有人会说自己毫无影响力。即使你觉得自己毫无权力，每个人都有一定的影响力，只要有影响力，就能践行这个原则。

（00:34:28）我和别人谈论商业时，无论是车库里的创业者，还是超级董事会、CEO、管理层之类的，我听到的都是同样的抱怨："埃里克，你说的这些太难了。现在你还要我额外努力？我已经要处理Vectura事件和其他事务了。我只是想安稳过一天。太难了。"

（00:34:53）但我认为这种看法本末倒置了。因为我问他们：有没有可能，商业之所以难，是因为没人信任你？如果人们信任你，或许会轻松许多。事实上，这不是假设，我们有确凿证据。员工信任公司的公司，沟通成本更低，团队更协调。客户信任公司，忠诚度更高，获客成本更低。犯错后，客户也更愿意留下来试用新产品。很多人总说"客户太善变了，没忠诚心，眼里只有竞争对手的花哨营销"。但或许把这些视为额外负担，恰恰是问题所在。

（00:35:46）"越难越容易"原则就是：如果你愿意前期投入精力专注于质量、设计、伦理、诚信、安全等事务（我不想定义你的价值观，由你自己说）；如果你在决策时坚守原则，就会获得意想不到的回报。但别为了回报而做，否则无效。你必须为了事物本身而努力。信任是商业中最被低估的资产。但从投资回报率角度看，信任创造的资产往往垫底，因为正确行事有无形回报，却有显性成本。

（00:36:28）再讲个例子。我们谈了这么多高深理论，现在讲点实用的。之前我提过Cloudflare。让我讲讲Cloudflare的故事。我喜欢这家公司，因为马修·普林斯和他的联合创始人坚决反对咨询公司那些废话。早期他们从哈佛商学院出来，深受其害。他们说："不，我们不想听什么使命宣言、价值观。我们只做防火墙和防护。"
云端服务。没那么复杂。我们不想听这些废话。" 所以多年来，他们一直没有制定使命宣言。（00:37:03）：这是一个关键点。作为领导者，我们过于专注于价值宣言和使命宣言，却忘记了使命宣言并非使命本身。地图并非领土。使命是我们所创造的生命体所自然涌现的特质。明白吗？这不是可以贴个标签就能了事的。你必须从内部去构建它。如果你希望公司坚守质量理念，就必须从内部培育这种理念。戴明在40年代就阐述过这一观点。这并非新奇想法，而是至关重要的理念。这才是工匠精神的真谛。好的。（00:37:32）：我们知道Cloudflare之所以能坚守使命，是因为他们经常会做一些看似更难实则更易的事。往往连他们自己都不明白原因。公司历史上有个著名的例子，民主抗议者——我记不清是哪个国家的——激怒了某个政府。为了不让抗议者协调民主活动，当局动用国家级黑客试图关闭他们的网站。（00:37:59）：Cloudflare这个小创业公司在硅谷四处奔波，恳求大科技公司帮助防御攻击。结果无人响应。连谷歌这样的巨头都表示"太害怕了"。Cloudflare毫不退缩："我们要承受国家级黑客的怒火来保护你们，因为这是正确的事。"

（00:38:26）：几年后，工程师们共进午餐时，有人问："你为什么喜欢在这家公司工作？因为这是我第一次感受到，我们在努力建设一个更美好的互联网。" 全桌人都附和："没错，建设更美好的互联网！" 有人问马修："这是我们的使命宣言吗？" 马修反问："不，我们没有使命宣言。我懂你们的意思，但不是的。"

（00:38:46）：但事实上这就是使命宣言。随着时间推移，工程师们不断重复"建设更美好的互联网"。这成了公司的口号。最终创始人不得不接受："好吧，就把这作为我们的使命宣言吧。" 这就是他们至今沿用的使命宣言。为了正式化价值观，公司规模扩大后这些东西变得至关重要。必须记录下这些涌现的特质，否则人们怎么能理解呢？他们的首要价值观是"秉持原则"，这才是真正更难也更易的做法。

（00:39:14）：这些听起来很棒。在不付出代价的情况下谈论价值观和使命宣言固然有趣，但有时代价高昂，可能会让生活更艰难。这就是为什么我们强调"更难也更易"原则。有一天，一个初级工程师——不是高管——走进马修·普林斯的办公室问："老大，我们的使命宣言不是'建设更美好的互联网'吗？" 作为CEO，任何以这种方式开场的对话都注定会带来额外工作。你只能回应："现在又怎么了？" 对方说："你不是在董事会上说过，我们推动营收增长、让用户从免费升级到付费的最大驱动力是什么？" 这是几年前的事了。
加密、SSL加密。你说这说得通，因为提供SSL加密服务成本很高，我们没法免费提供。我们得购买证书，支付相关费用，还要处理各种加密相关的工作……我们的计算资源本来就很有限，诸如此类的。" "好吧。"（00:40:08）："但老板，难道一个更好的互联网不应该是加密的互联网吗？" 他回答："没错。那你想说什么？" 所以如果加密更好，为什么我们要免费提供？很多人听过这个故事。如果你曾在公司担任中层管理者，肯定深有体会，每次有人走进办公室说‘老板，让我们免费提供产品吧’，你就得说：‘不行，我们有战略方向，专注核心业务。感谢你的意见，但我们有更重要的事要做。’（00:40:44）：所有人都以为马修会这样反应，这才是正常的。这是我们最赚钱的产品，你却说免费送人，走开吧。不行。马修告诉我，我亲眼见证了这个过程，印象深刻。他说了三个关键词：‘我们来想办法解决。’解决问题。这个‘想办法解决’的领导理念太强大了。（00:41:08）：如果你坚守某项原则，坚持质量至上等理念，生活注定会变得艰难。最优秀的领导者——那些我真正敬佩的人——会欣然接受这种挑战。他们热爱这种困难时刻，因为每当面临看似不可逾越的困境时，都是展示真正价值的机会。所以马修坚持让整个团队集思广益，如何免费提供加密服务。免费送肯定不行。他说：‘让公司破产可实现不了使命。’我们必须找到可持续的方案。我就不详细讲技术细节了。他们不得不手动编写软件和汇编语言代码，与证书机构达成复杂的商业合作。最终他们成功压低了成本。（00:41:48）：请记住，在任何时候……首先，我本可以用困难为借口放弃：‘太难了，做不到。’一旦他们成功了，本可以说：‘这只是免费利润，我们降低成本就能轻松赚钱。’上线时，他们得向董事会汇报转化率下滑的情况。当时付费用户增长放缓，几乎要放弃，但他们没有。他们坚守原则，因为这就是我们的立场。（00:42:15）：当然，故事有个圆满结局。用户增长量激增。直到今天，人们还在谈论Cloudflare如何让加密互联网成为理所当然。赢得的信任让他们如今市值达700亿美元。但大多数领导者被问及为何坚守原则时，都答不上来。因为他们被灌输了ROI至上、股东优先的思维，认为这是获取最大利润的唯一途径。（00:42:43）：作为对比，Groupon创始人安德鲁·梅森曾给我讲过另一个故事。大家还记得Groupon吗？可能现在不记得了。它已淡出公众视野，但曾是美国发展最快的私营公司之一。
这一切的核心在于每日推送的优惠邮件。Groupon每天只发送一封邮件，却成功上市了，可见其模式的成功之处。（00:43:06）我记得他曾跟我讲过这样一个故事：他的高管和员工开始频繁到办公室，跟他说：“老板，我们季度业绩要达标了，得多赚钱了。现在我们是上市公司，不能只发一封邮件。要不试试发两封？”他回答：“不行。一天一封邮件才是我们的核心策略。”但随着时间推移，员工们不断磨蚀他，开始用精益创业的术语说：“要不做个实验？看看数据？再考虑下投资者关系……回报率呢？”最后，他妥协了：“好吧，那就试试。”（00:43:38）结果发现，两封邮件确实能赚更多钱。他不得不妥协。然而好景不长，有人找到他说：“老板，两封邮件不够，应该发三封。”接着就发展到一天发八封邮件了。这不只是Groupon的例子。我遇到过太多CEO跟我讲同样的故事——邮件发送频率问题，似乎成了公司决策的试金石。人们总找不到合理的理由坚持正确的做法，结果就走上了歧途。短期内或许能赚大钱，但最终毁了整个公司。（00:44:13）所以，遵循“难者易之”的原则，是抵御公司丧失核心竞争力的第一道防线。

好吧，是的。所以再说一次，不行。写这份声明没有任何价值。明白吗？这份声明根本就不是它所声称的那样。我之所以用“道德准则”这个老派词汇，就是因为我试图在整本书中避免使用任何时髦的咨询术语。所以我尽量不使用“利益相关方”这个词，也不提“企业文化”。我就是想回归传统。（00:46:03）：这就是为什么我从“斯塔尔定价”说起。与其谈论利益相关方、使命宣言和价值观，我更想问：你们的受托人是谁？“受托人”这个词多土啊。但对我来说，每个领导者都必须回答这个问题，每个产品也必须回答这个问题：它的存在意义是什么？你宁愿死也不愿背叛的东西是什么？明白吗？（00:46:27）：如果你告诉我，我想做高质量的产品。我宁愿死也不愿推出劣质品。想想史蒂夫·乔布斯。他会为了电脑内部线路的排布和客户不应该拆卸看到的设计细节，和别人争得面红耳赤。这才是真正的工匠精神，对吧？难就难在必须做到完美。还有关于帕塔哥尼亚创始人伊冯·乔伊纳德的故事。如今他因环保行动更出名，但他曾是个质量狂人。他坚信质量是客观函数，每个产品都有应有的质量标准。大多数人觉得这很疯狂。但这正是帕塔哥尼亚成功的秘诀。这种理念太强大了。（00:47:06）：所以无论这个目标是什么，我们都必须将其编码到管理体系中，确保绝不会通过背叛原则来谋取私利。无论是在运营层面还是治理层面，这两点都至关重要。听我讲这些的人，有些可能会说：“目的？这不就是ESG那套废话吗？”好吧。

（00:48:51）：所以我们要做的第一步，也是最重要的技巧，就是明确“目的”是什么？你宁愿死也不愿背叛的东西是什么？必须写下来。必须像索尔·普莱斯那样，先把客户放在首位。
员工第二，股东第三。或者说伟大的彼得·德鲁克曾说过，这么做是本末倒置的。正确的顺序应该是员工第一，客户第二，股东第三。我不在乎你们怎么想，你们得把自己的信念写下来。（00:49:13）然后我们还要做一件事，我称之为"使命驱动"。那些声称以使命为导向的公司，大多数不过是怀揣使命的希望者而已。抱歉，这纯粹是扯淡。这不过是给掠夺性引擎披上糖衣外衣。我不买账。如果你们真心要践行使命驱动，就必须向我证明，除非完成使命，否则你们就无法盈利。这才是我们需要审计的重点。我们要审视，如果公司里有人动了削减质量、偷工减料、降低绩效、敷衍了事的念头……这些最容易被砍掉的项目——安全、绩效、质量、设计——往往最脆弱。创新，大概排第五。这就像末日四骑士一样，你把这些东西砍掉，短期内不会有太大问题。但信任的核心在于，我背叛了你，你甚至都察觉不到。（00:50:03）所以我们必须——
